  retry for ~7 minutes per URL. All results above therefore come from the repo issue-list route
  `https://github.com/{repo}/issues?q=...`, which stayed at HTTP 200 throughout. The `.../pulls?q=...`
  route renders a client-side React shell that failed with "Uh oh! There was an error while loading

It is filed only because the class (D.1 >1 GPU) technically applies; the quote contains no GPU-count words because the source expresses the requirement as a config value, not a count. STATED_REASON: "I was reporting per-stream `completion_tokens / (total − TTFT)`. When requests queue, fewer streams decode concurrently and each one's rate looks better. Measured as aggregate output tokens per second, 0.28 is **slower**, not faster."
S3B: NO-ACTIVE-WORK-FOUND (queries: `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q=is%3Aissue+benchmark+error+bars+confidence+interval` → 0 results; `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Aopen+benchmark+variance` → 0 results). The retraction is self-contained; no harness change to prevent per-stream-vs-aggregate mis-reporting has been proposed.
REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The trap survives — `vllm bench serve` still reports per-request TPOT and aggregate output throughput as separate fields, so the arithmetic error is a user-side hazard that no version bump removes. No expiry.

STATED_REASON: "My \"fixed\" harness counted `delta.reasoning_content`. In 0.28 the field is **`reasoning`** (`vllm/entrypoints/openai/engine/protocol.py:404` — `DeltaMessage` has `role/content/reasoning/tool_calls`). So thinking-enabled runs were still mis-timed."

subsection: paper's own throughput result does not isolate the thing it is named after
ARTIFACT: arXiv 2608.26389 — "LowRankArena: A Standardized Evaluation Platform for SVD-Based LLM Compression"
ARXIV_ID_READBACK: ARXIV_ID_READBACK: 2608.26389 — TITLE: LowRankArena: A Standardized Evaluation Platform for SVD-Based LLM Compression

QUESTION: Did the fused KDA-prefill kernels for ROCm ever land after the gfx90a build break?
ARTIFACT: PR #54038 — [ROCm][Perf] Kimi-K3 Fused kernels for KDA prefill reland
QUOTE: "#52606 added a KDA prefill fusion path for ROCm's gfx950, but was reverted in #53294 as its builds failed on gfx90a. This PR adds back the fused path, and guards the kernel builds on gfx950. This PR also adds a few optimizations to further improve the prefill performance, achieving ~5% TTFT reduction compared to the original triton path of the KDA prefill chain."

QUESTION: Was the FlashInfer block_size=16 / head_size=256 Blackwell workaround ever removable?
ARTIFACT: PR #36987 — [FlashInfer] Revert block_size 16 + head_size 256 workaround on Blackwell
QUOTE: "Since then, the upstream FlashInfer issue has been fixed and vLLM's FlashInfer dependency has been updated (in #30993) to a version that includes the fix (v0.6). The workaround is no longer necessary and can be safely removed."

QUESTION: Did the DeepGEMM-MoE default ever get changed for TP=8?
ARTIFACT: PR #29346 — [Perf] Disable DeepGEMM MoE by default when TP=8 is used
QUOTE: "Recent benchmarks have shown that the best performance for DeepSeek V3 TP=8 on Hopper/Blackwell is with VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0 VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 i.e. use DeepGEMM for the GEMM and Triton for the MoE. This PR sets that heuristic by default for any block fp8 model running at TP=8, which I think this fairly conservative."

QUESTION: Can async scheduling be left enabled for pooling models?
ARTIFACT: PR #39592 — [Pooling] Disable async scheduling by default for pooling models
QUOTE: "Asynchronous scheduling mostly benefits decode performance and as currently implemented can have a negative impact on TTFT. This means overall performance of pooling models is better without it enabled, so we'll disable it by default for now for these."

QUESTION: Did the FlashInfer fused add-RMSNorm + NVFP4 kernel ever ship?
ARTIFACT: PR #51925 — [Kernel] Enable optimized FlashInfer add-RMSNorm NVFP4 fusion
QUOTE: "In our Qwen3-30B profile, the fusion replaces 47 add-RMSNorm kernels and eliminates the corresponding 47 cvt_fp16_to_fp4 launches per forward pass."

QUESTION: Did CUDA-graph size defaults for v1 ever get settled?
ARTIFACT: contrast: PR #20062 / revert #20128
QUOTE: "Reverts #20062 as we would like to engage in further discussion on the 'right' default behavior" — the default was withdrawn rather than settled; see C4.x.

- **No genuine `wontfix` / `not planned` issue set in vLLM** — queries tried:
  `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+label%3Awontfix` (0 rows, "No results"),
  `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+label%3A%22not+planned%22` (0 rows),
  `https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+label%3Awontfix` (0 rows).
  The label set in vLLM (`/labels`) contains no `wontfix` / `not planned` label; the closes that exist are
  state-reason based and surfaced through `is%3Aunmerged` and `in%3Acomments` searches instead.
- **Explicit human "won't fix / by design" sentences are rare in both repos** — queries tried:
  `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q=is%3Aclosed+in%3Acomments+%22by+design%22`,
  `...%22we+will+not+support%22`, `...%22out+of+scope%22`, `...%22not+a+bug%22`, `...%22won%27t+fix%22`,
  `...%22no+plans+to%22`, `...%22working+as+intended%22`, `...%22unfortunately%22`,
  `...%22we+don%27t+plan%22`, `...%22decline%22`, and the same set for `sgl-project/sglang`.
  The hits are dominated by *closed-as-completed* issues (the report was a real bug and got fixed), not by
  refusals. Refusal-shaped reasons live almost entirely in *revert* PRs, which is why section C is
  weighted towards reverts.
- **`github.com/search?q=...&type=commits` (global commit search) is unreachable from this environment** —
  `python3 fetch.py raw 'https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Avllm-project%2Fvllm+%22Revert%22&type=commits'`
  times out (no bytes within 60 s; the global `/search` endpoint does not render server-side here).
  Revert mining was therefore done through the repo-scoped list search (`?q=Revert+in%3Atitle`), which works.
- **Local git history was not usable for revert mining** — `/tmp/vllm-0.28.0`, `/tmp/vllm_src` and
  `/tmp/sgl_src` are depth-1 clones (`git rev-list --count HEAD` = 1), so no `git log` revert archaeology.
- **Stale-closed items with a human reason: none kept** — the ~20 candidates whose only closure text was a
  `github-actions` / `stale[bot]` notice were dropped, as were the auto-revert PRs; see the drop accounting
  in each sub-researcher's NEGATIVE FINDINGS in C10/C11.
- **SGLang long-context attention (non-KV), benchmark methodology, tokenizer/detokenizer acceleration and
  CPU/host overhead yielded almost nothing human-closed** — see the NEGATIVE FINDINGS section carried over
  from S11-A at the end of C10.
- **Machine-authored auto-revert reasons are NOT human evidence** — 24 vLLM auto-revert PRs authored by
  `vllm-agent` (CI-failure analyzer) were segregated into C12 and excluded from every count.

Refusal-shaped reasons live almost entirely in *revert* PRs, which is why section C is weighted towards reverts. - **`github.com/search?q=...&type=commits` (global commit search) is unreachable from this environment** — `python3 fetch.py raw 'https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Avllm-project%2Fvllm+%22Revert%22&type=commits'` times out (no bytes within 60 s; the global `/search` endpoint does not render server-side here). Revert mining was therefore done through the repo-scoped list search (`?q=Revert+in%3Atitle`), which works. - **Local git history was not usable for revert mining** — `/tmp/vllm-0.28.0`, `/tmp/vllm_src` and `/tmp/sgl_src` are depth-1 clones (`git rev-list --count HEAD` = 1), so no `git log` revert archaeology. - **Stale-closed items with a human reason: none kept** — the ~20 candidates whose only closure text was a `github-actions` / `stale[bot]` notice were dropped, as were the auto-revert PRs; see the drop accounting in each sub-researcher's NEGATIVE FINDINGS in C10/C11. - **SGLang long-context attention (non-KV), benchmark methodology, tokenizer/detokenizer acceleration and CPU/host overhead yielded almost nothing human-closed** — see the NEGATIVE FINDINGS section carried over from S11-A at the end of C10. - **Machine-authored auto-revert reasons are NOT human evidence** — 24 vLLM auto-revert PRs authored by `vllm-agent` (CI-failure analyzer) were segregated into C12 and excluded from every count.

QUESTION: On sm120, which FlashAttention version does vLLM 0.29.0 actually select for dense attention — and does the "SM100+" wording in the docs hold on capability 12.0?
ARTIFACT: `vllm/v1/attention/backends/fa_utils.py::get_flash_attn_version` and `docs/design/attention_backends.md`, tag v0.29.0
QUOTE:
"        if device_capability.major == 9 and is_fa_version_supported(3):
            # Hopper (SM90): prefer FA3
            fa_version = 3
        elif device_capability.major == 10 and is_fa_version_supported(4):
            # Blackwell (SM100+, restrict to SM100 for now): prefer FA4
            fa_version = 4
        else:
            # Fallback to FA2
            fa_version = 2"
DETAIL: sm120 has major == 12, so it takes the `else` branch: **FA2**. The shipped docs state the rule more loosely — "Default is FA4 on SM100+ (Blackwell), FA3 on SM90 (Hopper), FA2 otherwise." — so the docs and the code disagree for major 12, and the code comment itself flags the gap: "(SM100+, restrict to SM100 for now)". The same file hard-gates FA4 by family: `return (fa_version == 3 and current_platform.is_device_capability_family(90)) or (fa_version == 4 and current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100))`, which is False on sm120 for both terms.

QUESTION: Which FlashInfer decode kernel exists on sm120, and does the TRT-LLM prefill kernel exist there too?
ARTIFACT: `vllm/utils/flashinfer.py` (v0.29.0) + `docs/design/attention_backends.md`
QUOTE:
"    SM90 (Hopper) and SM12x support the XQA decode kernel but not TRTLLM
    prefill. SM100+ supports TRTLLM for both phases. All others are unsupported."
DETAIL: The docs concur: "XQA is the SM90 decode path exposed through FlashInfer's TRTLLM decode API. trtllm-gen is used on SM100 and supports sinks." The decode-kernel selector in `vllm/v1/attention/backends/flashinfer.py` matches this: `if current_platform.is_device_capability(90) or current_platform.is_device_capability_family(120): return FlashInferDecodeKernel.XQA` followed by `assert current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100)`.

QUESTION: Is `torch.cuda.is_device_capability_family(100)`-style family checking true on sm120?
WHO: vLLM project (shipped API semantics) + reporter evidence on cc 12.x
ARTIFACT: `vllm/platforms/interface.py::is_device_capability_family` (v0.29.0) and issue #55397
QUOTE:
"        Returns True if the device capability is any <major>.x.
        Mirrors CUDA 13 'family' architecture semantics (e.g. 10.x, 11.x, 12.x)."
DETAIL: `return (current_capability.to_int() // 10) == (capability // 10)` ⇒ family(100) is **False** on sm120. Issue #55397 supplies the consequence table for NVFP4 kernel selection on cc 12.x: `FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4LinearKernel` gated by `is_device_capability_family(100)` is "**rejected** — family is 120", so selection falls through to `FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4W4A16LinearKernel`, which is accepted by an explicit `compute_capability in (100, 103) or 120 <= compute_capability < 130` clause; the native W4A4 CUTLASS kernel that "would pass" is "**never reached**".

"        # When `flashinfer_mxfp4` is enabled, dispatch to one of three FlashInfer

subsection: papers undercut by their own stated limitations
WHO: Dmitry Rybin, Yushun Zhang, Ding Tian, Zhihang Lin, Zhi-Quan Luo
ARTIFACT: arXiv:2510.05175 — "Exact Causal Attention with 10% Fewer Operations" (v3, 11 Oct 2025)
STATED_REASON: "We note that ECA cannot accelerate fused kernels such as FlashAttention on GPU. This is because ECA requires materialization of large intermediate expressions in the memory, while FlashAttention does not. However, it provides an alternative approach for compute-bound applications and can potentially be useful in scenarios with FLOPs considerations."
S3B: NO-ACTIVE-WORK-FOUND (queries: `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q="Exact Causal Attention" OR SparDA OR PersistentKV OR LycheeDecode OR TileMix OR RTPurbo` → 3 hits, none for ECA; no upstream implementation issue found in vLLM or SGLang trackers).
REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The blocking constraint is *algorithmic* (FLOP-reduction requires materialising intermediates that IO-aware kernels deliberately never materialise), not a compute-capability gate; nothing about sm120 or a newer FA would remove it. No sm120/CUDA-13 change found that revives it.

subsection: papers undercut by their own stated limitations
ARTIFACT: arXiv:2609.04105 — "Hardware-Aware FP4 FlashAttention-4" (3 Sep 2026)
STATED_REASON: "NVIDIA Blackwell executes 4-bit floating-point (FP4) matrix multiplication much faster than bfloat16 (BF16), but FP4 does not accelerate the work between those products." — and, from the results section: "This is also why fewer arithmetic instructions do not always help: independent arithmetic can occupy issue slots while the kernel is waiting for a dependency. 8.3 Takeaway 3: faster arithmetic does not scale the whole kernel". The paper also records a null hardware result: "In a matched control, reducing dynamic shared memory from 209,920 to 163,840 bytes did not improve latency because the 512-column TMEM allocation still allowed only one CTA per streaming multiprocessor." Its scope section states: "The noncausal model experiments are fixed-input inference evaluations rather than finetuning or pretraining studies."
S3B: NO-ACTIVE-WORK-FOUND (queries: `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q="FP4 FlashAttention" OR "flash attention 4" OR "flash attention 3"` → 12 loose hits, none an FP4-attention kernel port; the shipped sm120 attention paths are XQA decode + FA2, see A1.1/A1.2).
REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: Would expire if the softmax/conversion middle stage stopped dominating, e.g. on sm100 B300/GB300 (the paper notes "B300 and GB300 GPUs have doubled the exponential throughput to 32 ops / clock / SM, though these GPUs are not yet widely available at the time of writing"). **sm120 is not that hardware** and is not addressable by this method at all today, because FA4-class kernels are gated to capability family 100 in vLLM.

subsection: papers undercut by their own stated limitations
ARTIFACT: arXiv:2606.04511 — "SparDA: Sparse Decoupled Attention for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference" (3 Jun 2026)
STATED_REASON: "Even without prefetch, this variant already outperforms Sparse at B4 on both models because the Forecast indexer cuts block-selection latency; at this small batch, the prefetch pipeline adds slight overhead that makes the full SparDA marginally slower than the no-prefetch variant." The evaluation scope is also narrow by the authors' own account: "We report a single batch size of 4 because prefill throughput is insensitive to batch size, as GPUs are already fully utilized during the compute-heavy prefill phase."
S3B: OCCUPIED (open issue #48445) — `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q="Exact Causal Attention" OR SparDA OR PersistentKV OR LycheeDecode OR TileMix OR RTPurbo` returns "[RFC]: Support SparDA-style decoupled Forecast projection for lookahead KV prefetch in sparse attention" (#48445, opened Jul 13 2026, still open at retrieval).
REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The regression is batch-size dependent (the paper reports the full pipeline "pulls ahead of the no-prefetch variant" by B16 and is ~40% faster by B64), so the limitation would expire for a serving deployment at B≥16 — but *not* for the single-stream, batch-1 target of this rig. No sm120-specific revision found.

STATED_REASON: "PersistentKV is close to vLLM but does not beat FlashInfer on this roofline-style test. This result motivates the serving-system question: the advantage must come from low-active scheduling or page-aware execution, not from claiming a universally faster single-call kernel."

REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The claim is scoped by the authors to "commodity GPUs" and to a roofline-style isolated benchmark; it would expire if a scheduling-layer integration (not a kernel) were shipped in vLLM/SGLang. None found — the decode-kernel lead in these engines remains FlashInfer/XQA.

ARTIFACT: arXiv:2605.16928 — "Full Attention Strikes Back: Transferring Full Attention into Sparse within Hundred Training Steps" (v2, 8 Jun 2026)
STATED_REASON: "For long sequences, even sparse attention remains memory-bound because the selected KV blocks can still span tens of thousands of tokens." The paper's own limitation section adds: "10 Limitation Although RTPurbo achieves strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs, it still has several limitations. • Dependence on stable head specialization."
S3B: NO-ACTIVE-WORK-FOUND (queries: `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q="TileMix" OR "LycheeDecode" OR "RTPurbo"` → no hit; `...?q="Exact Causal Attention" OR SparDA OR PersistentKV OR LycheeDecode OR TileMix OR RTPurbo` → 3 hits, none RTPurbo).
REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The bound is a bandwidth argument (sparse selection still streams a large KV working set), so it would only expire with a change in the memory system or a harder sparsity budget — not with sm120. Note the paper also *requires a training phase* (head specialisation is learned), which is itself a limitation class the brief asked about.

ARTIFACT: arXiv:2607.08786 — "Accelerating GPU Inference of Large Language Models with Moderately Unstructured Sparse Weight Matrices" (13 Jun 2026)
STATED_REASON: "Our scheme does not outperform FlashLLM ( Xia et al., 2023 ) under high sparsity. The limitation arises from the storage format, as most regions require zero padding while few contain surplus non-zeros, rendering our redistribution strategy ineffective." The same section reports a second loss: "In this compute-bound regime, our design, optimized for memory-bound decoding with small N N , runs slower than cuBLAS ( Nvidia, 2025b ) ." (spacing/`N N` duplicated in the retrieved HTML rendering).
S3B: NO-ACTIVE-WORK-FOUND (queries: `https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q="FlashLLM" OR "SparDA" OR "PersistentKV"` → no FlashLLM hit; `...?q=SageAttention` → no port of this format).
REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The paper's own diagnosis is that the *format* is the problem, and it notes a compute-bound regime inversion (slower than cuBLAS). A denser/sparser hardware path (e.g. block-scaled FP4 tensor cores on sm100/sm120) could change the regime; no work found that ports this scheme onto it.

STATED_REASON: "As shown in Figure 5 , while the configuration with 4/8 sparse heads exhibits latency comparable to or slightly underperforming the dense FlashAttention-2 baseline, all other settings with a higher degree of sparsity consistently and significantly outperform it." The conclusion concedes deployment readiness: "Finally, while we have achieved considerable speedup, our method is not yet integrated with highly optimized inference serving frameworks like vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) , which is left for future work."

WHO: authors of arXiv:2606.07713 ("Attention at the Theoretical Minimum")
ARTIFACT: arXiv:2606.07713 — "Attention at the Theoretical Minimum: A Mathematics of Arrays Framework for Memory-Optimal Transformer Kernels" (5 Jun 2026)

STATED_REASON: "Piecewise pieces are replayed reading their inputs from the addresses recorded at capture time; CUDAGraphWrapper deliberately does not copy inputs (per its docstring). If a producer feeding a piece returns freshly-allocated outputs — e.g. an op added to splitting_ops that doesn't write into persistent buffers, such as vllm::moe_forward_shared (its outputs are fresh torch.empty_like tensors; it declares no mutates_args and no out-variant, unlike the attention ops which write persistent buffers) — those outputs land at new addresses every step, so the downstream piece replays reading stale memory and silently corrupts output."

QUESTION: Which INT4 weight-only kernels exist for sm120 — Marlin vs Machete?

STATUS: shipped (Marlin built for 12.0; Machete is Hopper-only by construction)
QUOTE:
"    # The machete kernels only work on hopper and require CUDA 12.0 or later.
    # Only build Machete kernels if we are building for something compatible with sm90a
    cuda_archs_loose_intersection(MACHETE_ARCHS \"9.0a\" \"${CUDA_ARCHS}\")"
MARLIN-FP8_(same_file,_verbatim):
"    # - sm90 and sm100 don't support QMMA.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3 SAAS instruction

So on sm120: `gptq_marlin` / `awq_marlin` W4A16 exist, **Machete does not**, and an FP8-input Marlin

QUESTION: Why does sm120 get treated as "sm100" by some vLLM gates and not others?
WHO: vLLM contributor bojiang3 (merged) + the `Platform` interface docstring
ARTIFACT: vLLM PR #54306 "[Bugfix] Gate sm_100-only kernel tests on the capability family, not >=" (MERGED); `vllm/platforms/interface.py`
STATUS: merged (capability-family semantics are now the documented check)
QUOTE: "has_device_capability(100) is a >= test, so a device reporting capability 12.1 satisfies it. Tests that guard sm_100-only kernels with it therefore run on consumer and workstation Blackwell, where those kernels do not exist, and fail instead of skipping."
SECOND_(same_body,_verbatim): "is_device_capability_family(100) is the check these guards want. Its docstring states the difference:"
THIRD_(interface.py,_verbatim):
"        Returns True if the device capability is any <major>.x.
        Mirrors CUDA 13 'family' architecture semantics (e.g. 10.x, 11.x, 12.x)."
_rawblock: Consequence measured in the same PR body: "test_cutlass_mla_decode.py | 49 failed | 49 skipped"; "test_trtllm_nvfp4_moe.py | 1 failed | 1 skipped". 65 call sites of the family predicate exist in v0.29.0; the linear-kernel gates that exclude sm120 by family are `nvfp4/flashinfer.py` ("FlashInfer cutedsl requires sm_10x"), `mxfp8/flashinfer.py`, `online/nvfp4.py` (raises `"nvfp4_per_token online quantization requires a Blackwell (SM100) GPU."`), while `nvfp4/flashinfer.py`'s `>=sm_100` sibling gate and `nvfp4/marlin.py` do admit 12.0.

QUESTION: At model scale, which of FP8 / INT8 / INT4-weight-only is actually lossless, and what does the largest FP4 study conclude?
WHO: Kurtic, Marques, Pandit, Kurtz, Alistarh (Neural Magic / IST Austria); Egiazarian et al. (IST Austria / Red Hat)
ARTIFACT: arXiv:2411.02355 ""Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death"? Accuracy-Performance Trade-Offs in LLM Quantization"; arXiv:2509.23202 "Bridging the Gap Between Promise and Performance for Microscaling FP4 Quantization"
QUOTE: "(1) FP8 (W8A8-FP) is effectively lossless across all model scales, (2) well-tuned INT8 (W8A8-INT) achieves surprisingly low (1-3\%) accuracy degradation, and (3) INT4 weight-only (W4A16-INT) is more competitive than expected, rivaling 8-bit quantization."
SECOND_(2509.23202_abs_page,_verbatim): "Yet, their practical benefits remain unproven. We present the first comprehensive study of MXFP4 and NVFP4 for post-training quantization, revealing gaps between their promise and real-world performance. Our analysis shows that state-of-the-art methods struggle with FP4, due to two key issues: (1) NVFP4's small group size provably neutralizes traditional outlier mitigation techniques; (2) MXFP4's power-of-two scale quantization severely degrades accuracy due to high induced error."
_rawblock:
(2411.02355 ran >500,000 evaluations on the Llama-3.1 family through vLLM. The same 2509.23202 page
reports 4x end-to-end on an RTX 5090 — see C10 for the tension.)

QUESTION: Does RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell have the same FP4 throughput as B200?
ARTIFACT: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition product page; getdeploying.com B200-vs-RTX-PRO-6000 comparison
QUOTE: "4000 TOPS 1,2" with, verbatim, "1. Peak rates based on GPU Boost Clock. I 2. Theoretical FP4 TOPS using sparsity."
AGGREGATOR_PAGE_(blog/aggregator,_verbat: "9,000 TFLOPS" (B200) vs "2,000 TFLOPS" (RTX PRO 6000) and "4.5x higher on B200"; FP8 "4,500 TFLOPS" vs "1,000 TFLOPS"; "Bandwidth 7,700 GB/s vs 1,597 GB/s  4.8x higher on B200".
_rawblock:
Answer: **No.** The sm120 part has FP4 tensor cores, but ~4.5x lower dense FP4 throughput and
~4.8x lower DRAM bandwidth than B200. Every FP4 speedup number measured on B200/H100 in the
literature is therefore not transferable to this rig (see A1.14 and C11 for sm120-measured data).

QUESTION: Can quantization be applied on the fly at load time without a pre-quantized checkpoint or calibration data, and what does `--quantization fp8` actually do on this version?
ARTIFACT: `docs/features/quantization/online.md` (main) + `llm_compressor/fp8.md` (v0.29.0); `vllm/config/quantization.py` `_ONLINE_SHORTHANDS`
QUOTE:
"Online quantization lets you take a BF16/FP16 model and quantize its Linear
and MoE weights to lower precision (such as FP8) at load time, without needing
a pre-quantized checkpoint or calibration data. Weights are converted during
model loading and activations are dynamically scaled during each forward pass."
ON-THE-FLY_FLAG_(v0.29.0_fp8.md,_verbati: "In this mode, all Linear modules (except for the final `lm_head`) have their weights quantized down to FP8_E4M3 precision with a per-tensor scale. Activations have their minimum and maximum values calculated during each forward pass to provide a dynamic per-tensor scale for high accuracy. As a result, latency improvements are limited in this mode."
_rawblock:
`fp8_dynamic` EQUIVALENT (config/quantization.py, verbatim comment above the shorthand): "    # Per-output-channel weight scale + dynamic per-token activation.
    # Same shape as llmcompressor's FP8_DYNAMIC recipe.
    \"fp8_per_channel\": QuantizationConfigArgs("
Scheme list in v0.29.0: `fp8_per_tensor`, `fp8_per_block`, `fp8_per_channel`, `mxfp8`, `mxfp4`,
`int8_per_channel_weight_only` (MoE only), `nvfp4_per_token` (MoE only, Blackwell SM100 only).
`--calculate-kv-scales` is KV-adjacent and excluded from this map.
_extra: `fp8_dynamic` EQUIVALENT (config/quantization.py, verbatim comment above the shorthand): "    # Per-output-channel weight scale + dynamic per-token activation. # Same shape as llmcompressor's FP8_DYNAMIC recipe. \"fp8_per_channel\": QuantizationConfigArgs(" Scheme list in v0.29.0: `fp8_per_tensor`, `fp8_per_block`, `fp8_per_channel`, `mxfp8`, `mxfp4`, `int8_per_channel_weight_only` (MoE only), `nvfp4_per_token` (MoE only, Blackwell SM100 only). `--calculate-kv-scales` is KV-adjacent and excluded from this map.

QUESTION: Is chunked prefill on by default in vLLM V1, and what does the scheduler do with a mixed pool of prefill and decode requests?
ARTIFACT: `docs/configuration/optimization.md` §"Chunked Prefill" (vLLM v0.29.0)
QUOTE: "In V1, **chunked prefill is enabled by default whenever possible**. With chunked prefill enabled, the scheduling policy prioritizes decode requests. It batches all pending decode requests before scheduling any prefill operations. When there are available tokens in the `max_num_batched_tokens` budget, it schedules pending prefills. If a pending prefill request cannot fit into `max_num_batched_tokens`, it automatically chunks it."

QUESTION: What is the documented rule for choosing `max_num_batched_tokens`?
ARTIFACT: `docs/configuration/optimization.md` §"Performance Tuning with Chunked Prefill"
QUOTE: "- Smaller values (e.g., 2048) achieve better ITL because there are fewer prefills slowing down decodes.\n- Higher values achieve better time to first token (TTFT) as you can process more prefill tokens in a batch.\n- For optimal throughput, we recommend setting `max_num_batched_tokens > 8192` especially for smaller models on large GPUs."
NOTE: the documented recommendation is a strict inequality `> 8192`, and (see A.4.4) the *default* selected for a ≥70 GiB non-A100 card in the OpenAI-server usage context is exactly `8192` — i.e. one token below the documented throughput recommendation.

QUESTION: When a request has encoder (multimodal) inputs, how does the scheduler decide which encoder items to run in the same step as decoder tokens?
ARTIFACT: `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` (vLLM v0.29.0)
QUOTE:
"An encoder input will be scheduled if:
        - Its output tokens overlap with the range of tokens being computed
        in this step, i.e.,
        [num_computed_tokens, num_computed_tokens + num_new_tokens).
        - It is not already computed and stored in the encoder cache.
        - It is not exist on remote encoder cache (via ECConnector)
        - There is sufficient encoder token budget to process it.
        - The encoder cache has space to store it.

        If an encoder input cannot be scheduled due to cache or budget
        limitations, the method adjusts `num_new_tokens` to schedule only the
        decoder tokens up to just before the unschedulable encoder input."

WHO_IS_STILL_ASKING: quocdat029x (contributor) — vLLM PR #56238 "[Bugfix][Metrics] Anchor queue time at the first QUEUED event"
ASKING_QUOTE:
"IterationStats.update_from_events overwrites queued_ts on every QUEUED event, but update_from_finished_request computes

 # Queued interval is from first QUEUED event to first SCHEDULED 
 queued_time = req_stats . scheduled_ts - req_stats . queued_ts"
WHAT_IS_MISSING: The registered metric documents itself as "time spent in WAITING phase for request", but the computation subtracts a `queued_ts` that the event loop overwrites on every QUEUED event, so a request that re-enters the waiting queue (e.g. after preemption) reports a queue time anchored at its *last* queue entry rather than its first. REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The measured +0.2% result was taken on **Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on L40S** against the `AsyncScheduler` of that date. The RFC's own "When This Would Help" section names the untested regime — "Multi-tenant RAG with N distinct system prompts where N > KV cache capacity / prompt_blocks — forcing eviction competition between tenant prefixes". On a single 96 GB card with a 4B model the KV pool is very large relative to a 4B model's per-token footprint, so the eviction-competition precondition is *even less* likely to hold than on L40S; the reason is therefore unlikely to have expired in the direction that would revive this. Separately, the successor design (#53277, still open) narrowed the target to cache-warm continuation under long-context contention.

A complete fix needs to preserve eager SWA memory reclamation while avoiding chunk-sized fallback, likely through component-specific reuse/replay (full-attention KV reusable through `B`, with only the missing SWA tail rebuilt) or an explicit checkpoint mechanism."

The 32,000-token shared prefix ends inside the fourth chunk, before its retained SWA tail. Matching consequently falls back to 24,576 cached tokens and prefills 9,424 tokens (7,424 remaining shared-prefix tokens plus the 2,000-token unique suffix) instead of only 2,000."

The regression is attributed to unified-cache/SWA behaviour and to `chunked_prefill_size` 8192 not dividing the 32,000-token prefix — and 8192 is *also* the SGLang 0.5.19 auto-default chosen for a 96 GB card (A.4.11). The reason has therefore very likely expired *for this rig's model*, while the chunk-boundary observation about `chunked_prefill_size` remains live.

The PR (#32710) notes end-to-end benchmarking as a \"planned follow-up\" — this is an independent data point for that."

REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: None identified. The reported finding is a live caution, not an expired one.

subsection: vLLM "only schedule prefill chunks when the entire context fits" — PR closed unmerged; the idea later shipped by another route
WHO: jmkuebler (PR author); vLLM maintainers closed PR #21809 unmerged
ARTIFACT: vLLM PR #21809 "[Bugfix] Scheduler: only schedule prefill chunks when entire context fits" (state token `CLOSED`; not merged)
STATED_REASON_(verbatim_from_the_PR_body: "I observed that v1 behaves weirdly when preempting long context requests when prefix caching is disabled and chunked prefill is enabled, see #18115 . The root cause is that the v1 scheduler preempts requests when KV cache is full (intended) but then immediately tries to reschedule them based only on the next chunked prefill step size, not checking if there's enough memory for their entire existing context. This creates a cycle where requests restart, partially fill memory, get preempted again, and repeat indefinitely (not intended)."
SECOND_QUOTE_(same_body,_verbatim,_the_g: "More generally, unless we do prefix caching, we should not schedule prefill chunks unless the full context will be able to fit. Otherwise, those request get preempted and we thrash the compute (and added latency for the other running requests)."
MEASURED_SYMPTOM_(same_body,_verbatim): "Before fix the generation throughput drops and the KV utilization oscillates, because the preempted requests wrongly schedules chunks again. The preempted request never enters the waiting state"
S3B: SOLVED (shipped in v0.29.0 by a different route — the `scheduler_reserve_full_isl` config field, whose v0.29.0 docstring is verbatim: "If True, the scheduler checks whether the full input sequence length fits in the KV cache before admitting a new request, rather than only checking the first chunk. Prevents over-admission and KV cache thrashing with chunked prefill." It defaults to `True`. Query used: `is:issue "cache affinity scheduler"` and the v0.29.0 source read of `vllm/config/scheduler.py`, which was searched independently of PR #21809's own citations.)
REASON-MAY-HAVE-EXPIRED: The reason has expired. PR #21809 was written against a V1 scheduler that admitted a chunk without checking whether the request's whole context would fit; vLLM v0.29.0 ships exactly that check as `scheduler_reserve_full_isl: bool = True`, default on. The thrash cycle described in the PR body is guarded against by default in the rig's version.

subsection: D.1 >1 GPU
WHO: vLLM issue #41682 reporter; environment is a multi-GPU PP deployment
ARTIFACT: vLLM issue #41682 "[Bug]: Pipeline Parallelism scheduler does not split sequences into pipeline micro-batches"
HARDWARE_QUOTE: "- Hardware: NVIDIA GB300 (SM103) NVL72\n- Model: DeepSeek-R1-0528-FP4\n- Workload: ISL = 128K, OSL = 1, aggregated mode, single 4-GPU node"
SECOND_HARDWARE_QUOTE_(the_reproduction_: "Configuration: `--pipeline-parallel-size 4 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-batched-tokens <chunk>`. Sweep `<chunk>` over {4K, 12K, 32K} and compare against no-chunk baseline. All other knobs identical."
WHY_RULED_OUT: the defect only exists when `pipeline-parallel-size > 1`; the rig has one GPU. The chunk-size sweep is the strongest published single-source evidence that chunked prefill can *cost* throughput, but it is not attributable to a single-GPU configuration.

subsection: D.1 >1 GPU
ARTIFACT: vLLM issue #51743 "[Bug]: DeepSeek-V4-Flash TP on H100: --max-num-batched-tokens >= 24576 crashes EngineCore in fused qnorm/rope/kv-insert op; allocation ..."
HARDWARE_QUOTE: "- 4x H100-80GB (HBM3), single node, `--tensor-parallel-size 4`"
WHY_RULED_OUT: the fault is in a TP-sharded fused op (`fused_deepseek_v4_qnorm_rope_kv_rope_quant_insert`) reached only under tensor parallelism; the rig is TP=1. Also model-gated (DeepSeek-V4-Flash MLA), not Qwen3-4B.

subsection: D.1 >1 GPU AND D.2 >96 GB VRAM
ARTIFACT: vLLM issue #51454 "[Performance] DP8 vs TP8 for single-KV-head MLA: 7.7x KV, 3.4x faster 1M TTFT at c=8 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, 8x B200, vLLM v0.25.0)"
HARDWARE_QUOTE: "On a single 8x NVIDIA B200 node, `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.25.0` serves `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` (304B total / 13B active, MLA, 1M context, FP4 experts + FP8 KV) with measured multi-session 1M-context concurrency that has not been published before for this model class."
WHY_RULED_OUT: the headline (DP8 vs TP8 KV replication) is a multi-GPU parallelism-shape question and the node has 8×~180 GB. The rig has one 96 GB card, where the TP-vs-DP question does not arise.
RELEVANT_MEASURED_NEGATIVE_RESULT_CARRIE: "Increasing `--max-num-batched-tokens` beyond 8192 yields no TTFT improvement and costs 32% of KV capacity."

subsection: D.1 >1 GPU; D.4 prefill/decode disaggregated service
WHO: SGLang issue #38478 author; measurement taken on a prefill-only disaggregated deployment
ARTIFACT: SGLang issue #38478 "[Feature] Scheduler: opt-in NO_TOKEN admission lookahead with head-prefix pinning (head-of-line relief for prefill)"
HARDWARE_QUOTE: "Instrumenting the admission loop on a prefill-only H100 TP=8 deployment with hierarchical cache showed that passes ending in `NO_TOKEN` with an empty batch were ~45 % of all idle scheduler rounds."
SECOND_HARDWARE_QUOTE_(verbatim): "A/B on the same deployment (500 requests, long shared-prefix multi-turn sessions, two rounds each, gate off vs `N=4`, aging 20):"
WHY_RULED_OUT: the headline idle-rate figure is measured on a **prefill-only** node inside a PD-disaggregated service with **TP=8**, a deployment shape the rig cannot host (one GPU, no second node, no fabric). The *mechanism* (the `break` on `AddReqResult.NO_TOKEN` in `get_new_batch_prefill`) is present in the single-GPU path too — which is why the same finding is also filed above as B.4.3 — but the 45 % idle-round measurement is not transferable to this rig.

- **`max_num_partial_prefills` does not exist in vLLM 0.29.0.** It appears nowhere in `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py`, `vllm/config/scheduler.py`, or `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` at tag `v0.29.0`, and nowhere in a local `vllm` main checkout. - **`--num-lookahead-slots` does not exist in vLLM 0.29.0.** Same evidence path: 0 matches for `num_lookahead_slots` in the local checkout and absent from the v0.29.0 scheduler/config/arg_utils. The V1 scheduler allocates lookahead internally via `num_lookahead_tokens` derived from the speculative config, not from a CLI flag.
- **`--disable-chunked-prefix-cache` is SGLang-only and is documented as a DeepSeek-specific overhead saving, not a general knob.** Its v0.5.19 help string is "Disable chunked prefix cache feature for deepseek, which should save overhead for short sequences." No general-purpose "disable chunked prefix cache" mechanism was found on the vLLM side under that name.
- **No vLLM issue or PR was found that documents an accepted *method* for picking `max_num_batched_tokens`.** The only shipped guidance is the three-line tuning rule in `optimization.md` (A.4.2) plus the memory/name ladder in `get_batch_defaults` (A.4.4). Is it for delta update optimization?", "What are the differences between stop and abort? Can we merge the two functions?") and no statement of why it was closed. QUESTION: Is grammar compilation in vLLM cached, bounded, and off the critical path — and how is the compile pool sized on a many-core host?
ARTIFACT: `VLLM_XGRAMMAR_CACHE_MB` (default 512 MB) + async grammar-compilation `ThreadPoolExecutor`
QUOTE: "The default max_workers if not specified is the number of CPUs * 5, which is way too high since these tasks are CPU-bound, not I/O bound. We also know we would never dominate CPU usage with just grammar compilation, so we set it to half the number of CPUs."
SOURCE_FACT_(same_file_/_`backend_xgramm: `grammar_init()` submits every request's compile to that executor (`self.executor.submit(self._create_grammar, request)`) unless the distributed backend is `external_launcher`; the xgrammar compiler is built with `cache_enabled=True, cache_limit_bytes=vllm.envs.VLLM_XGRAMMAR_CACHE_MB * 1024 * 1024`; `VLLM_XGRAMMAR_CACHE_MB` reads `os.getenv("VLLM_XGRAMMAR_CACHE_MB", "512")`.
RIG_CONSEQUENCE: the pool is `max(1, (cpu_count + 1) // 2)` → **~104 compile workers on this 208-core host**, uncapped and cgroup-unaware; the measured consequence of that sizing in production is issue #49460 (see B5.3).
EXTERNAL_CORROBORATION_(arXiv_IDs_read_b: arXiv:2601.04426 "XGrammar-2: Dynamic and Efficient Structured Generation Engine for Agentic LLMs" — "XGrammar-2 introduces TagDispatch for dynamic structural dispatching and Cross-Grammar Cache for substructure-level cache reuse across grammars." ; arXiv:2608.03065 "Efficient Grammar-Constrained Decoding via Parser Stack Classification" — "the online computational overhead of existing GCD methods, with latency typically scaling linearly with vocabulary size, limits the throughput of LLMs, especially for models with large vocabularies." and "PSC computes masks up to 700$\times$ faster than baselines on complex programming language grammars, and up to 30$\times$ faster for schema-conformant JSON".

QUESTION: How expensive is the per-decode-step structured-output bitmask on the host, and was the resulting regression fixed?
WHO: vLLM (reporter romancomplexio; root-caused and fixed by njhill in #49919)
ARTIFACT: issue #49013 ("[Perf] ~2x decode throughput regression for structured outputs since #45424") + PR #49919 ("[Core] Explicitly manage torch CPU threads in workers")
QUOTE: "torch defaults its intra-op thread pool to the host core count, ignoring process affinity, cgroup CPU quotas, and co-located worker processes. Any torch CPU op above the parallel_for grain size (32k elements) fans out across that pool, and the OpenMP workers then spin-wait after every parallel region - stealing cycles from the engine loop's serial code and, in containers, burning the CFS quota so that the entire process is throttled for the rest of the quota period. This is the root cause of the 2-6x structured-output decode throughput regression reported in #49013 (per-step pinning/fill of the ~12.6MB grammar bitmask on the hot path)."
RESIDUAL_(reporter,_verbatim,_after_the_: "unfortunately, this hasn't fixed the performance regression. In my understanding the problem for us has been the added allocation of a 12MB tensor per every structured decode step."
NOTE: the merged fix addressed thread oversubscription, not the per-step allocation; the two PRs that targeted the allocation directly (#49150, #49780) were closed unmerged with no stated reason (see NEGATIVE FINDINGS). This is the single largest measured per-step non-GEMM cost in this file, and it is CPU-side, not GPU-architecture-specific.

QUOTE: "vllm:model_execute_time_milliseconds (Histogram) - The time spent in the model execute function. This will include model forward, block/sync across workers, cpu-gpu sync time and sampling time."
QUOTE_2: "These metrics are only enabled when OpenTelemetry tracing is enabled and if `--collect-detailed-traces=all/model/worker` is used."

Sampling time appears only inside the OTel-gated `model_execute_time_milliseconds` bucket, where it cannot be separated from GEMM time.
QUOTE_4_(why_finer_timings_were_not_adde: "We already have `inference_time` and `decode_time` metrics, so the question is whether there are sufficient common use cases for the higher-resolution timings to justify the overhead."

subsection: D.1 >1 GPU — grammar compilation/masking is per-TP-rank work
WHO: tlysanhuo (PR author), SGLang; original designs by raayandhar (#13947) and hnyls2002 (#16874)
ARTIFACT: PR #38392 "perf: compile grammars and apply vocab mask only on the entry TP rank" (closed unmerged); re-landed as open PR #39053; predecessor #16874 "Reintroduce compiling grammar on TP0" still open
HARDWARE_QUOTE: "With TP > 1 and no speculative decoding, every TP rank currently compiles the same grammar (the backend cache is per-process, so caches never converge across ranks) and computes/applies the grammar vocab mask at every decode step. The sampler then keeps ranks in sync via all_reduce(MIN) , which depends on bitwise-deterministic sampling kernels — the original motivation of the sampling_info.grammars special case. Re-lands #13947 (reverted by #16845 because DP attention was broken), following up on the stalled #16874 , ported to the current GrammarManager structure."
WHY_RULED_OUT_ON_THIS_RIG: the optimization is defined by "TP > 1" — with one GPU there are no peer ranks whose duplicate compiles or vocab-mask work can be deduplicated, and the `all_reduce(MIN)` sync it targets does not exist. The single-GPU cost of grammar masking is the per-step bitmask path instead (A5.9).

subsection: D.1 >1 GPU — sampling is a collective across vocabulary shards
ARTIFACT: Issue #54333 "[RFC]: Reduced sampling for tensor-parallel decoding"
HARDWARE_QUOTE: "Tensor-parallel vocabulary projection produces one vocabulary shard per TP rank. The current sampling path gathers all shards before selecting the next token, resulting in `O(B × V)` communication per sampling step. This is unnecessary for several common workloads: - Greedy decoding only needs the global argmax. - Bounded top-k sampling only needs the global top-k candidate set. - Greedy speculative verification only needs one target argmax per position. This RFC proposes a gener..."
WHY_RULED_OUT_ON_THIS_RIG: the cost described is `O(B × V)` cross-rank communication that exists only when the vocabulary is sharded across TP ranks; with a single GPU there is exactly one shard and the saving is zero.

QUESTION: Why do the vLLM authors consider per-step CPU tensor construction in Python a first-order problem, and what did they build to remove it?
WHO: vLLM maintainers (Model Runner V2 design doc)
ARTIFACT: `docs/design/model_runner_v2.md` § "1. Persistent Batch"
QUOTE: "V1 introduced persistent batches to minimize CPU overhead during input preparation. When requests are scheduled for a step, the model runner must construct contiguous input tensors (for example, block tables and per-request temperature values) to feed into the model. Building these tensors from scratch each step is often very slow in Python, especially for large tensors like block tables."

QUESTION: Does an over-large PyTorch/OpenMP intra-op thread pool measurably slow the engine loop, and what is the shipped fix?
ARTIFACT: PR #49919 "[Core] Explicitly manage torch CPU threads in workers"
QUOTE: "torch defaults its intra-op thread pool to the host core count, ignoring process affinity, cgroup CPU quotas, and co-located worker processes. Any torch CPU op above the parallel_for grain size (32k elements) fans out across that pool, and the OpenMP workers then spin-wait after every parallel region - stealing cycles from the engine loop's serial code and, in containers, burning the CFS quota so that the entire process is throttled for the rest of the quota period."
NOTE_(second_continuous_quote_from_same_: "After warmup completes in compile_or_warm_up_model() : set torch threads to 1. No steady-state CPU op benefits from intra-op parallelism; it only creates spin-wait contention and quota burn."

QUESTION: Was there a measured per-step CPU regression from building/pinning a host tensor inside the decode step, and how big was it?

QUESTION: Is `pin_memory()` in the per-step H2D path free, or does it cost host time under concurrency?
ARTIFACT: PR #37006 "[V1] Remove pin_memory() in async_copy_to_gpu to fix sporadic stalls"
QUOTE: "Under sustained high-concurrency workloads (e.g., TTS serving at 24+ concurrent requests), x.pin_memory() in async_copy_to_gpu causes sporadic stalls of up to ~12ms per call. This is because pin_memory() calls cudaHostAlloc() under the hood, which takes a global lock in the CUDA driver to pin pages in physical RAM. Under concurrency, threads serialize on this lock."

QUESTION: Does vLLM's own documentation treat the API-server / HTTP process as a performance-relevant cost, or does the project claim the HTTP layer is free?
ARTIFACT: `docs/configuration/optimization.md` § "CPU Resources for GPU Deployments" (v0.29.0)
QUOTE: "Using fewer physical CPU cores than processes will cause contention and significantly degrade throughput and latency. The engine core process runs a busy loop and is particularly sensitive to CPU starvation."
QUOTE-2: "- **Output processing** -- detokenization, networking, and especially streaming token responses use CPU cycles"
QUOTE-3: "If you observe that GPU utilization is lower than expected, CPU contention may be the bottleneck. Increasing the number of available CPU cores and even the clock speed can significantly improve end-to-end performance."
NOTE: The same section names "tokenization, chat template rendering, and multi-modal data loading" as CPU-resident input-processing work. This is the project's own statement that the front-end is a first-class cost, i.e. it is evidence *against* an unqualified "the HTTP layer is not the bottleneck" claim.
S3B: SOLVED (shipped in v0.29.0 ; verified present at line 424+ of the v0.29.0 doc)

QUESTION: Is there a supported way to scale the HTTP/API layer independently of the engine, and why does it exist?
WHO: Nick Hill (njhill), merged by vLLM maintainers
ARTIFACT: PR #17546 "[Perf] API-server scaleout with many-to-many server-engine comms" + `--api-server-count`
QUOTE: "A new --api-server-count arg to vllm serve can be used to specify an arbitrary number of API servers to run. When used in conjunction with --data-parallel-size there's all-to-all zmq-based communication between API servers and data parallel engines."
QUOTE-2: "When deploying large DP sizes using this method, the API server process can become a bottleneck. In this case, the orthogonal `--api-server-count` command line option can be used to scale this out (for example `--api-server-count=4`)."
S3B: SOLVED (merged #17546 ; flag `--api-server-count` present in vLLM 0.29.0 `vllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py`)

QUESTION: How expensive is an "optional" FastAPI middleware in the vLLM HTTP layer, measured?
ARTIFACT: PR #19946 "[Perf][Frontend]: eliminate api_key and x_request_id headers middleware overhead"
QUOTE: "The current implementation for the middleware that handles authentication (--api-key) and X-Request-Id headers (--enable-request-id-headers) uses a high level abstraction provided by FastAPI that allows middleware to be written as functions with access to the Request object. This causes an unacceptable performance hit when the middleware is installed."
QUOTE-2: "As can be seen, ~10% decrease in throughput is huge for the little computation that is actually done when enabling both middleware."
NUMBERS_(verbatim_tables_in_the_PR_body): before — without middleware 94.8 QPS, `--api-key` 90.6 QPS (-4.4%), `--api-key` + `--enable-request-id-headers` 85.5 QPS (-9.8%); after pure-ASGI rewrite — 94.0 / 93.8 (-0.2%) / 93.3 (-0.7%). The PR also removes the documentation warning that `--enable-request-id-headers` has a performance penalty at high QPS.
S3B: SOLVED (merged #19946)

WHO: Ray Serve / Ray LLM users and maintainers, ray-project/ray issues #52746 and #59681
ARTIFACT: Issue #52746 "[ray.serve.llm] serve.llm with streaming has overhead compared to vllm-v0 for a single replica when concurrency > 32" ; Issue #59681 "Additional Overhead in Ray Serve LLM than Bare vLLM images"
STATED_REASON: "**Isolating the overhead: it's the HTTP layer, not Ray Core**"
SECOND_QUOTE_(same_comment,_the_measured: "The actor wrapper introduces effectively zero overhead. The entire ~100ms gap lives in the HTTP/routing path — `proxy.py` → `router.py` → `replica.py`."
THIRD_QUOTE_(same_comment,_the_environme: "Tested with vLLM (Qwen3-0.6B) on a single replica, batch size 32, RTX 4090."
FOURTH_QUOTE_(#59681,_the_second_measure: "There is a ~200token/s total throughput decrease in Ray Serve LLM.(~30 tok/s difference in output throughput). 2. Continuing on the above, ~20ms increase in mean TTFT and ~50ms in P90 TTFT."

STATED_CAVEATS_(verbatim,_#59681): "Caveats: small model on a consumer GPU makes fixed overheads proportionally more visible than on large models; single node, one replica."
ADDITIONAL_CAVEAT_(#52746,_the_baseline_: "VLLM_USE_V1=\"0\" vllm serve unsloth/llama-3-8b-Instruct --tensor-parallel-size 1  --disable-log-requests" — the vLLM baseline was run on the **V0** engine with request logging disabled, so the reported gap is not a v1-vs-Serve-LLM comparison and the baseline excludes request-logging cost.

The dominant fixed cost in #59681 was the response `Batcher` waiting out `MODEL_RESPONSE_BATCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 50 ms); the reporter measured that setting it to 0 drops TTFT p50 64.8 → 26.3 ms, and #64534 was opened to flush the first result immediately. The maintainer's remedy ("direct streaming") changes the recommended configuration, so the *default* numbers in these issues may no longer reproduce. The residual high-concurrency tail (TTFT 71 → 330 ms at c=32, 114 → 758 ms at c=64, throughput 5518 → 3634 tok/s) was explicitly flagged by the reporter as "architectural ... rather than a single fixable defect" and remained open at the time of the thread.
S3B: SOLVED for the fixed-cost half (reporter-opened fix #64534 plus the maintainer-recommended direct-streaming configuration) / NO-ACTIVE-WORK-FOUND for the concurrency-scaling half (queries: `https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+serve+llm+streaming+overhead`; `https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+%22direct+streaming%22`)

WHO: Euijun Chung, Yuxiao Jia, Aaron Jezghani, Hyesoon Kim — "Characterizing CPU-Induced Slowdowns in Multi-GPU LLM Inference"
HARDWARE_QUOTE: "Large-scale machine learning workloads increasingly rely on multi-GPU systems, yet their performance is often limited by an overlooked component: the CPU."

The engine-side segmentation vLLM does publish (`QUEUED`/`SCHEDULED`/`NEW_TOKENS`) is documented in `docs/design/metrics.md` but explicitly starts at tokenization. - **Any metric, in either engine, for sampling time or detokenization time** — nothing found.
